items.content_excerpt: Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . items.content_excerpt: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. items.title: Show HN: KradleBench – Multi-agent AI evals in Minecraft
items.summary: Hi HN - This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you! Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds. 1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property. 2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies. 3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too. Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety. Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals. We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens. Thanks for reading, James & Kemal

items.title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
items.summary:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.

In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.

Reviewing code is hard

Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.

To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:

  1. LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.
  2. LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.
  3. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes.

How Sashiko reviews a patch

To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Gather context and plan\r\n -> Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)\r\n -> Triage\r\n -> Per-bug deep checks\r\n -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f42d1205150>)])]>

Notes on each step:

  1. Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.

  2. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.

  3. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.

  4. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.

  5. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.

All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.

What the data shows

The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.

It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle.

It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization.

Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic.

Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%.

A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). 

That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch.

This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch:

"As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds (on lore.kernel.org)

What we learned from building and running Sashiko

First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level).

Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced.

Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning, Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers.

More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration.

Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git.

"Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML

You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev, or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.

items.title: Show HN: Intrusive.ai – open-source AI attack simulation
items.summary: I created the INTRUSIVE.AI platform to give agent builders the ability to evaluate their agents against OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications (and more generally, just to allow for comprehensive testing in a non-production environment). Through my own experience with evaluating agents, I found indirect prompt injection testing to be especially difficult due to the architectural nature of it. To overcome that challenge, I created Interceptor Sandbox - a sandbox that runs agents in a simulated environment where all of the services an agent might rely on (HTTP, MCP, Postgres/pgvector to name a few) can be "intercepted" via an injection API to inject malicious payloads. Interceptor Sandbox: https://github.com/intrusiveai/interceptor_sandbox Additionally, I found that existing open source AI testing and attack simulation solutions didn't provide the breadth of capabilities I needed so I created Attack Harness for that purpose. But it also had to be sandboxed because any sufficiently capable attack harness can't be trusted to play nice once it's been given nefarious goals and so that led to Operator Sandbox. I haven't seen other people talking about the sandboxing method that I've employed in Operator so it seems to be a somewhat novel approach that might shake up the way people are thinking about sandboxing AI agents. Operator Sandbox: https://github.com/intrusiveai/operator_sandbox The full suite is documented here: https://docs.intrusive.ai The platform is still very much in its alpha stage so your mileage may vary but I would sure appreciate any feedback that comes my way. Feel free to use GitHub Issues on the respective repos to provide feedback.

We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. items.summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.
items.story_key: story|title:langsmith for coding agents now track spend by outcome
items.content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Install

Python wheels

Platform Install

CUDA 13.0 (uv) uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto
ROCm 10.0 pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100
XPU uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

latest tags work the same way (e.g. vllm/vllm:latest-rocm). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The -efa image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576).

  • Model Runner V1 removed (#63373).
    • VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER and VllmConfig.use_v2_model_runner are gone; setting the env var to anything but 1 fails at startup.

  • Default --block-size is 64 instead of 16 (#63231). Backends with a preferred block size still override it (ROCm paged attention keeps 16), and an explicit --block-size still wins.
  • gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 when unset with the extensible KV cache on (#56492). An explicit value in (0.8, 1.0) that withholds 1 GiB or more logs a warning (#66704).

items.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
items.story_key: story|title:why your fine tuning job takes longer than the flops say
items.content_excerpt: Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models . The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. items.title: Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue
items.summary: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic task allocation under partial observability, we introduce a communication-augmented Bayesian task-allocation framework. Our agent uses dialogue to reduce uncertainty about the environment and collaborators, while keeping decisions grounded in explicit probabilistic beliefs. We evaluate our framework in an Overcooked domain extended with dynamically arriving tasks under both full and partial object-space observability. Our communication agent consistently outperforms a vanilla LLM agent in both settings. Additionally, our framework performs comparably to a non-communicating task-allocation baseline under full observability, but substantially outperforms it under partial observability as task complexity increases by an average speed up of 0.585 and completes on average 18 timesteps faster. These results indicate that our agent is more efficient in dynamic task allocation than baselines in partially observable environments, and that communication is important as available information decreases.

items.title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
items.summary: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.

items.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

Most AI assistants can read a person's email, files, and calendar, but it can't tell which revenue table is certified or how finance defines net retention. This leads to inconsistent outcomes, low adoption, and a lack of trust among business users. Genie Ontology solves this context problem for Genie by combining the business semantics teams explicitly define with context learned from everyday work, so answers are grounded in a full understanding of the business. Once that context is unified, the next step is putting it to work. As AI assistants and agents spread across the business, organizations need to control data access, spend, and tool usage at scale. Without that control, sensitive data can reach the wrong people, AI spend becomes hard to predict, and agents can connect to tools no one has approved. In Genie, Unity Catalog enforces each user's data permissions, and Unity Gateway gives admins the traces, MCP policies, and budget controls they need to manage AI across the organization. Genie brings both essential context and governance into the Microsoft tools your teams already use with the Azure Databricks Genie plugin, which connects Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Cowork to Genie One. items.title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
items.summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
items.story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
items.content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time.   • [VSCode] Fixed the diff tab not opening for multi-line edits on files with CRLF line endings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation continuing to record after switching sessions
  • [VSCode] Improved sign-in errors behind TLS-inspecting proxies: a certificate failure now says what to do, as the terminal does
  • [VSCode] Changed opening a Claude Code on the web session in a folder where Claude Code's sandbox is on: the extension no longer switches to the session's branch for you, and the dialog says why
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the message when a file fails to upload to a cloud or Remote Control session: it now gives the reason, such as too many pages, a password or a time-out
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved adding a repository Claude can't access to a cloud session: a short message and a Reconnect GitHub button replace the long error
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed self-hosted sessions staying on "Starting Claude Code" after it had started, when you reopened a paused session without sending a message
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed a paused session in a self-hosted environment sometimes still showing "Sending" and a Stop button under the "Session paused" banner
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed pull request updates from GitHub Enterprise Server linking to github.com in cloud sessions; new updates link to your own server
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the message when some network secrets can't be added to a new cloud environment: it lists each host, says why where it can, and stays until you dismiss it
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed very large GitHub Actions job logs and run log archives failing to download or being cut off in cloud sessions
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the new-session repository picker when GitHub single sign-on hides organizations: it now says so even with other repositories listed, and links to reconnect GitHub
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions started from the iOS app with a repository not getting a branch of their own
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an open cloud or Remote Control session's page staying "Disconnected" after a few minutes of failed connections; it now tries to reconnect by itself
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed Try again on an open cloud or Remote Control session's "Connection lost" card sending "Try again" as your message; it now tries to reconnect instead
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed the Stop button disappearing from a cloud session five minutes into a reply that had shown nothing yet while Claude was still working
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an approval prompt sometimes disappearing from a tab left open after a self-hosted runner released the session while it waited for your answer
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a failure notification when a scheduled task's run can't start because its settings require a sandbox that isn't available where it runs
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the Git providers page when your GitHub sign-in has expired: it now asks you to reconnect instead of silently hiding organizations you can link
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed removing a repository from a scheduled task silently moving its GitHub trigger to another repository; Save now waits until you pick one
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed git clones and fetches that take longer than ten minutes in a cloud session sometimes being cut off at the very end
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added the No repository option to the repository picker for new sessions on a self-hosted environment
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a warning to a cloud session's Delete dialog when deleting it will pause scheduled tasks that run in that session
  • [Remote Control] Fixed your own session saying its environment was deleted when you deleted nothing; it now says your computer is no longer connected
  • [Remote Control] Fixed some sessions still showing as running in the session list after the computer disconnected before Claude started; they now show an error mark or as idle
  • [Remote Control] Added a Try again button to the error shown when the computer running your session is signed out of Claude Code
  • [Claude Tag] Added Claude Tag sessions started in Slack to the Compliance API on Enterprise plans, in beta: list the sessions and read their transcripts
  • [Claude Tag] Added a confirmation step when an admin turns off Claude Tag for the organization, with a dialog that says what stops
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed scheduled tasks in a Slack channel moved between Enterprise Grid workspaces failing to use Slack until someone posted there
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Approve and post card in a DM with Claude appearing for private or Slack Connect channels, where Claude can't post; Claude now gets the reason and shows no card
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Retry button to a Slack channel's Configure page for when its settings fail to load
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Scope filter to the Network events tab of Claude Tag's Activity page, so admins can download one scope's events instead of the whole organization's
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Remove connector in Claude Tag admin settings being refused when access bundles also held its credentials; it now removes those set on the connector and leaves the bundles' own
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Channels tab in Claude Tag admin settings splitting a workspace from its channels across pages; channels now appear right under their workspace
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Set for Claude Tag link on the Cloud environments admin page not leading to the environment setting; it now opens the Slack page's Advanced tab, where you set it
  • [Code Review] Added a Download CSV button to Code Review admin settings: export review costs per repository by month, week or day, for one repository, one GitHub organization or all
